Modern.brandNameRationale: Single word. Ship is the verb every modern product team lives by. The brand sits on the daily action of getting work in front of users. Plain, modern, immediately legible to anyone who has worked in software.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern SaaS has matured into a category with strong design conventions and a few dominant patterns. The customer is design-literate and impatient with anything that feels enterprise-stale. The opening is for a small product brand that talks like a product team and ships like one.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Linear (linear.app) holds the design-led product peer position. Notion (notion.so) sits in the workspace tier. Vercel (vercel.com) holds the developer-platform peer. Height (height.app) does the modern issue-tracking middle. We sit closest to Linear in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A product tool for teams that already ship and want a tool that doesn't slow them down.

Modern.tagline: The plain verb. The whole product.
Modern.brandNameRationale: One word. Ship is what every product team is trying to do and most days fail to. We named the product after the verb on the whiteboard so the name itself is a small reminder. It is also unowned in SaaS — the obvious word nobody has taken.
Modern.manifesto: Most product tools ask you to set up the tool before you can use it. Boards, fields, automations, integrations, a quarter of onboarding. We made SHIP because the only question that matters on a Tuesday is what is going out this week. Type the work, mark it shipped. That is the loop. Everything else is decoration.
Modern.industrySummary: Project tooling for product teams is bloated. Linear opened a lane for taste and speed; everyone else added more surface. There is a smaller, quieter market underneath Linear for a tool that does one thing — track what is shipping this week — and refuses to grow.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Linear (linear.app) holds the speed and craft slot. Height (height.app) and Shortcut (shortcut.com) fill the middle. Trello (trello.com) is the floor. We sit underneath Linear with a deliberately smaller surface — a single weekly view, a single keyboard, and almost no settings.
Modern.positioningStatement: SHIP is a one-screen product tracker for teams that just want to know what is going out this week.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on what we left out. The product is a list, a status, a keyboard. The pricing is one tier. The marketing is the changelog.

messagingPillars.name: Changelog as marketing

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Hartshorn is an old English place and surname with a quiet, slightly archaic register — the opposite of every modern SaaS naming convention. Software is the plain category word. The pair feels like a small firm that decided to opt out of the tech-naming arms race, and that decision is the brand.
Luxury.story: Hartshorn Software was founded by three engineers who had spent years inside larger software companies and wanted to build a smaller catalog of tools, more carefully. The company ships one major version per year. The team is intentionally small. The customers are loyal across decades.
Luxury.industrySummary: Most premium B2B software signals premium by being expensive. There's a smaller market for software that signals premium by being restrained, slow-roadmap, deeply documented, and built to last a decade. We belong there.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: JetBrains (jetbrains.com) holds the closest peer in seriousness and restraint. Panic (panic.com) sits in the craft-led peer position. Tinderbox (eastgate.com) does the heritage indie-software middle. We sit in their company.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small software house for teams that buy slowly and stay long.

Luxury.tagline: One major release a year. Built to outlive your laptop.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: A surname with a small-firm register, plus the plain category word. The 'Co.' signals an older species of company — a partnership, not a venture-funded sprint. The customer reading the name should picture a workshop, not a product launch.
Luxury.story: Pemberton was founded by two engineers who left a large platform company to make smaller, more durable software. The first product took three years to ship. It is on version 7 and the original buyers are still on it.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium B2B software has become synonymous with high pricing and high churn. There is a quieter market for software priced like furniture: bought once, kept for a decade, deepened slowly with one annual release.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: JetBrains (jetbrains.com) sets the bar for serious indie tooling. Panic (panic.com) holds the craft slot. Tinderbox (eastgate.com) and OmniGroup (omnigroup.com) are the heritage indie peers. We belong with them, not with the VC-backed cohort.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Pemberton makes software the way good firms make furniture: one piece at a time, slowly, and for a long life.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We ship one major version per year. We do not chase feature parity. We keep customers across decades by being worth keeping, not by switching costs.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Docs is the most basic word for what a great deal of software is actually about: the document. The brand sits on the smallest unit of work, plain and unadorned.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most document and writing software is feature-heavy and slightly bloated. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the document, the cursor, and the page.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most writing tools fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some Japanese text-editor traditions and certain minimalist editors like iA Writer (ia.net) and Bear (bear.app).
Minimal.positioningStatement: A writing tool that does writing. That is the entire product.

Minimal.tagline: An instruction, not a product name.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: One word. The verb that completes the sentence the customer is already inside: 'I should just use…' We picked the verb and stopped. The label inside the app says USE. The browser tab says USE. The brand is the instruction.
Minimal.manifesto: Software brands work very hard to convince you to start. Onboarding tours, sample data, badges, streaks. We made USE because the customer already knows they need this. The whole job of the brand is to get out of the way so the using can begin.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most SaaS adds onboarding to make activation metrics look healthy. The minimal-tool market — Notion in early days, Bear, iA Writer — proves the opposite works. There is room for a brand that takes the minimal premise further than anyone.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: iA Writer (ia.net/writer) is the closest peer in restraint. Bear (bear.app) holds the friendly minimal slot. Linear (linear.app) is the maximal version of taste. We sit further out than Writer — fewer features, less branding, no marketing site to speak of.
Minimal.positioningStatement: USE is the tool you reach for when you do not want to think about the tool.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip every product element that asks for the user's attention. No streaks. No empty states with art. No feature releases. The tool opens, the work begins.

Corporate.tagline: Enterprise workflow software for regulated industries.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Lattimer is a surname pulled from a 1960s engineering firm that built control systems. Systems Group is the category. The pair signals a serious vendor — the kind a procurement team enters into a master agreement with, not a tool a developer signs up to with a credit card.
Corporate.manifesto: We build software for the part of the enterprise where downtime has a number attached. The buyer is a director of operations, not a head of growth. The contract is three years, not three months. We ship slowly and predictably because the customer's calendar runs on slow, predictable cycles.
Corporate.industrySummary: Regulated industries — healthcare, financial services, energy, defense — are mid-cycle on a workflow software refresh. The legacy vendors are tired. The cloud-native vendors are not enterprise-ready. The opening is for a serious, deliberate mid-vendor with the discipline of the incumbents and the architecture of the cloud-native cohort.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: ServiceNow (servicenow.com) is the incumbent. Pegasystems (pega.com) holds the workflow-platform middle. Appian (appian.com) is the modern alternative. We sit underneath them, narrower and deeper, focused only on regulated workflow.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Lattimer Systems Group provides workflow software for regulated industries — built for audit, change-control, and procurement realities.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Our differentiator is the parts of enterprise software the customer never sees in a demo: audit trails, role separation, environment promotion, vendor security review. We ship those first and the workflow surface second.

Creative.tagline: We caught it in code review.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Three words. Off By One is the classic programming bug: the loop that runs one too many or one too few times. The brand puts the smallest, most universal engineering mistake in the brand position. Loud, self-aware, and immediately legible to any developer.
Creative.manifesto: Most software brands sell perfection: the seamless workflow, the zero-bug release, the magical transformation. We made Off By One because the actual experience of software is debugging the small mistake nobody caught. The brand is for the engineers who know that the work is mostly in the corrections, the version increments, the patches that nobody announces.
Creative.industrySummary: SaaS branding has been polished, transformation-led, and slightly anxious. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about the actual quiet work of building good software.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Linear (linear.app) holds the design-led restraint peer. Vercel (vercel.com) sits at the modern monochrome tier. Cursor (cursor.com) does the modern dev-tool middle. Tailscale (tailscale.com) holds the warm-technical peer. We sit warmer than all of them, with a clearer point of view.
Creative.positioningStatement: A SaaS brand for engineers who know the work is mostly in the corrections.

Creative.tagline: We ship when it's ready. We are mostly not ready.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words that say no to the whole genre. Slow Software is the opposite of every value SaaS markets on — fast, real-time, instant, AI-powered. We made the opposing case the name of the company. Reads as a quiet provocation.
Creative.manifesto: Every software company markets the same way: we are fast, we are getting faster, we are using AI to be even faster. We started Slow Software because the work we want to do — and the work our customers want to do — is not actually faster when the tool is faster. The work is slower. The tool should match.
Creative.industrySummary: Productivity software has confused speed with quality. The customer who notices the difference is rare, but real, and currently underserved. There is room for a brand that takes the opposite side of every SaaS argument and treats slowness as a feature.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Cortado (cortado.app), Daylight (daylightcomputer.com), and the Reflect (reflect.app) cohort touch the slow-tech edge. We are louder and more opinionated than any of them — the name is the position.
Creative.positioningStatement: Slow Software is a workshop building deliberately slow productivity tools — for people who think the speed is the problem.
Creative.positioningRationale: We make the case for slowness explicit in everything: the name, the manifesto, the release cadence, the support hours. Customers self-select.
